reason: The goal starts with glucose after a meal, and the pancreatic cells are shown beside blood vessels, so they seem like a sensible place to follow the response.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will respond to the glucose-rich blood.

effect: The meal's glucose is now shown in the whole body; the pancreatic response appears to come later.
reaction: I expected the sensing cells to respond directly, so the required body step was a little surprising.
reason: The body now has rising blood glucose, and the pancreatic cells are positioned to sense it.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will respond to rising blood glucose.

effect: The pancreatic cells release insulin into blood, with routes toward muscle and liver.
reaction: The marked routes make the next connection clearer.
reason: The insulin route points toward muscle, which is available as a separate closeup.
expectation: Insulin will signal the muscle to take up glucose from the blood.

effect: Insulin helped muscle take up glucose, and the next goal is to keep glucose available between meals.
reaction: It is clear how the response helps lower the rise after eating.
reason: The clock represents the time when incoming glucose decreases, matching the new goal.

choice.combine: Body taking up glucose into muscle

expectation: The body will move to a between-meals state as its cells continue using glucose.

effect: Blood glucose has fallen between meals, while the liver still has stored glycogen.
reaction: The picture makes the stored fuel relevant to the new goal.
reason: The pancreatic sensing cells responded to rising glucose, so I expect them to detect the fall too.
expectation: The pancreas will respond to the falling blood glucose.

alternatives.reason: The liver could release stored glucose, but a sensing step may come first.

effect: Lower blood glucose led pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon, which travels toward the liver.
reaction: The marked route makes the liver connection clear.
reason: The glucagon route points to the liver, and the earlier liver chapter showed glycogen being broken down to release glucose.
expectation: Glucagon will signal the liver to release glucose from its stored glycogen.

effect: The liver released glucose from glycogen, and glucagon release decreased as blood glucose rose. Both chapter goals are complete.
reaction: The before-and-after sequence made the feedback response clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting glucagon to the liver was most worthwhile: it showed how stored glycogen helps keep glucose available between meals and how the response eases afterward.

leastWorthwhile.text: Putting meal glucose into the whole body first felt less worthwhile because I expected the sensing cells to respond directly.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the first attempt needed the body as an intermediate; compatibility feedback completed that step automatically.

arbitrary.text: The initial body prerequisite was not obvious to me, though the feedback showed what to do. The later muscle and liver connections had clearer purposes.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: comparing the after-meal and between-meal responses made the connections between organs understandable, though the intermediate body step was less clear.
